lessons.title: Introduction and Why It Matters
lessons.body: In metal casting, your furnace must reach the melting point of the metal you are pouring. Aluminium melts at around 660Â°C, while cast iron needs about 1200Â°C. The fuel you choose and how you burn it determines whether you succeed or waste time and money. In many African workshops, charcoal, coal, and firewood are common, but they have different heat values and burn rates. For example, charcoal burns hotter and cleaner than wood, but it is more expensive. Coal can produce high heat but often contains sulphur that can ruin your metal. Understanding fuels and combustion means you can pick the right fuel for the job, control the air supply to get complete burning, and avoid excess smoke or dangerous gases. This module will teach you how to select, store, and use fuels efficiently. You will learn to build a fire that reaches the right temperature, how to tell if combustion is complete by the flame colour, and how to save money by using less fuel. Whether you are melting scrap aluminium for cooking pots or casting bronze for art, mastering fuels and combustion is the difference between a successful pour and a failed one.

lessons.title: Tools and Materials
lessons.body: To work with fuels and combustion, you need more than just a match. Start with a metal drum or clay furnace. A 200-litre steel drum cut in half works well for small melts. You need a tuyere (a pipe that blows air into the fire), which can be made from a 2-inch steel pipe. A blower or bellows is essential: a hand-cranked blower from a blacksmith or a simple vacuum cleaner motor can work. For fuels, you need charcoal (preferably hardwood charcoal), coal (bituminous or anthracite), or coke. Avoid wet wood. You also need a fire rake or long-handled tongs to move fuel, a metal bucket for ash, and a pyrometer or thermocouple to measure temperature if you can afford one. A cheaper alternative is to learn the colour of hot metal: dark red is about 600Â°C, bright orange is 900Â°C, and yellow-white is 1200Â°C. Safety gear: leather gloves, face shield, and a respirator mask for fumes. For storage, keep fuel dry in a covered shed. In Africa, you can often find charcoal at local markets, and coal from hardware stores or mining areas. Always have a fire extinguisher or sand bucket nearby. Remember, the right tools make the job faster and safer.

lessons.title: Step by Step Method
lessons.body: Step 1: Prepare your furnace. Place it on a fireproof surface, away from walls. Step 2: Lay a bed of small kindling (dry wood shavings or paper) at the bottom. Step 3: Add charcoal or coal on top, leaving space for air. Step 4: Light the kindling from the bottom through the tuyere hole. Step 5: Once the fire catches, turn on the blower slowly. Too much air at first will blow out the fire. Step 6: Add more fuel gradually as the fire grows. Keep the fuel bed about 15-20 cm thick. Step 7: Watch the flame. A yellow-orange flame means incomplete combustion; add more air. A blue flame means complete combustion and maximum heat. Step 8: For melting aluminium, you need about 700Â°C. For cast iron, 1200Â°C. Use a pyrometer or watch the crucible colour. Step 9: Once the metal is molten, skim off dross (impurities) with a skimmer. Step 10: Pour carefully. Always keep the blower running until you finish. After pouring, shut off the air and let the fire die. Never pour water on a hot furnace. In Africa, many foundries use charcoal because it is locally available. But charcoal burns fast, so you must keep adding it. Coal burns longer but needs more air. Practice with small batches to learn your fuel's behaviour.

lessons.title: Common Mistakes and Fixes
lessons.body: Mistake 1: Using wet fuel. Wet wood or charcoal produces steam, lowers temperature, and creates smoke. Fix: Store fuel under cover for at least a week before use. Mistake 2: Not enough air. Without enough oxygen, fuel burns slowly and produces carbon monoxide. Fix: Check your blower and tuyere for blockages; increase air flow gradually. Mistake 3: Too much air. This blows heat away and can extinguish the fire. Fix: Adjust the air supply until you see a steady blue flame. Mistake 4: Using the wrong fuel for the metal. Charcoal may not reach 1200Â°C for cast iron. Fix: Use coke or coal for high-melting metals. Mistake 5: Adding large chunks of fuel at once. This smothers the fire. Fix: Add small amounts frequently. Mistake 6: Ignoring smoke colour. Black smoke means incomplete combustion and wasted fuel. Fix: Improve air supply or use drier fuel. Mistake 7: Not cleaning ash. Ash blocks air flow. Fix: Remove ash after every melt. Mistake 8: Leaving fire unattended. Fix: Always have someone watching. In Africa, a common mistake is using charcoal made from softwood, which burns quickly. Fix: Buy hardwood charcoal from reputable sellers. Also, don't use petrol or kerosene to start the fire; it's dangerous. Use paper and kindling instead.

lessons.title: Safety and Best Practice
lessons.body: Safety starts before you light the fire. Wear cotton or wool clothing, not synthetic, which melts. Leather boots, gloves, and a face shield are must-haves. Set up your furnace in a well-ventilated area, ideally outdoors or with a chimney. Carbon monoxide is invisible and deadly; never work in a closed room. Keep a bucket of sand, a fire extinguisher, and a first-aid kit within reach. Before lighting, check that the tuyere and blower are clear. Never use petrol, diesel, or paraffin to start a fireâuse paper and kindling. When adding fuel, use long-handled tongs; never use your hands. Stand upwind to avoid smoke and heat. If you smell sulphur (like rotten eggs) from coal, stop and move to fresh air; it can cause health problems. For best practice, preheat your crucible gradually to avoid cracking. Keep the fuel bed even. Monitor the flame: a blue flame is efficient and safe; a yellow flame means you are wasting fuel and creating soot. After the melt, let the fire burn out completely. Dispose of ash in a metal container, not plastic. In Africa, many foundries use charcoal, which produces less sulphur than coal. But charcoal still produces carbon monoxide. Always have a buddy systemânever work alone. Teach others about safety. Remember, a safe foundry is a productive foundry.

lessons.title: Practical Exercise
lessons.body: Exercise: Melt 1 kg of scrap aluminium using charcoal in a small drum furnace. You will need: a 100-litre drum, a 2-inch steel pipe for tuyere, a hand blower or hair dryer (on cold setting), 3 kg of hardwood charcoal, a crucible, tongs, and safety gear. Step 1: Set up the furnace on bare ground. Step 2: Fill the drum with a layer of kindling and 1 kg of charcoal. Step 3: Light the kindling and start the blower slowly. Step 4: After 5 minutes, add more charcoal. Step 5: Place the crucible with aluminium scrap in the fire. Step 6: Keep the blower running. Watch the flame: it should become blue. Step 7: After about 15-20 minutes, check if the aluminium is molten (it will look like shiny liquid). Step 8: Skim off dross. Step 9: Pour into a preheated mould. Step 10: Shut off the blower and let the fire die. Record how long it took and how much charcoal you used. Compare with coal: repeat the exercise using coal. Which fuel gave a faster melt? Which was cheaper? In Africa, charcoal is often easier to find, but coal may be cheaper per kilogram. Calculate your cost per melt. Also, observe the smoke: charcoal produces less smoke. This exercise teaches you to control air, fuel type, and temperature. Do it three times to improve your speed. Always keep safety first.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Fuels and Combustion in African Foundries

Whether you are running a small jua kali workshop in Gikomba, a metal fabrication cluster in Nnewi, or a growing foundry in Ogun State, the fuel you burn and how you burn it will determine your melt quality, your production cost, and your profit margin. This practical reference consolidates the technical data, conversion factors, and troubleshooting guidance you need to make fast, informed decisions on the foundry floor. It is written for the operator, the workshop owner, and the technician who must keep the furnace running and the costs down.

Fuel Selection at a Glance

African foundries typically rely on one of four fuel pathways: coke (metallurgical or foundry coke), charcoal, diesel, or liquefied petroleum gas (LPG). Each has different calorific values, ignition characteristics, and cost structures. The choice is rarely purely technical â it is a business decision shaped by local supply chains, transport costs, and the scale of your operation.

Table 1: Comparative Fuel Data for African Foundry Operations

Fuel Type Net Calorific Value (MJ/kg) Typical Cost (USD/tonne, 2024) Best Use Case Key African Supply Regions
Foundry Coke 28â31 350â550 Cupola melting, large-scale iron casting South Africa (Mpumalanga), Zimbabwe (Hwange), Nigeria (Enugu)
Charcoal (hardwood) 28â33 150â300 Small crucible furnaces, non-ferrous melting Kenya, Tanzania, Ghana, Uganda, Zambia
Diesel 42â45 900â1,200 Rotary furnaces, crucible heating, backup melting All urban centres; price varies by country subsidy
LPG 45â50 800â1,500 Aluminium and brass melting, clean combustion needs Nigeria, Kenya, South Africa, Egypt, Ghana

Sources: Calorific values from Combustion and Incineration Processes (W.R. Niessen, CRC Press, 4th ed., 2010), Table 3.4; cost ranges compiled from regional supplier surveys and Africa Energy Portal (African Development Bank, 2024). Prices are indicative and vary significantly by location and order volume.

Table 2: Combustion Troubleshooting Guide

Symptom Likely Cause Quick Fix Business Impact
Yellow, smoky flame with black tip Insufficient air / rich fuel mixture Open air blast valve 10â15%; check tuyere blockage Higher fuel consumption; 5â10% cost increase per melt
Melt takes longer than normal Wet fuel, low calorific value, or excessive charge weight Switch to dry fuel stock; reduce charge size; preheat charge Lost production time; 20â30% throughput reduction
Excessive slag build-up High ash content in coke or charcoal; flux imbalance Add limestone flux (2â5% of charge); source cleaner fuel Frequent tapping delays; increased labour cost
White, hard iron / poor fluidity Low combustion temperature; excessive air blast cooling Reduce blast volume; increase coke-to-metal ratio Rejected castings; 15â25% scrap rate increase
Backfire or puffing at charging door Trapped gases; insufficient bed height Increase coke bed height by 150â200 mm; charge slowly Safety hazard; possible operator injury and equipment damage

Sources: Adapted from Principles of Metal Casting (R.W. Heine, C.R. Loper, P.C. Rosenthal, McGraw-Hill, 3rd ed., 2010), Chapter 8; and practical field notes from foundry operations in Kenya and Nigeria (Rise Africa Skills internal training data, 2023).

â  SAFETY WARNING â Carbon Monoxide (CO) Poisoning

Carbon monoxide is odourless, colourless, and potentially fatal. It is produced in large quantities during incomplete combustion in cupolas, crucible furnaces, and charcoal stoves. In enclosed or poorly ventilated workshops â common in dense urban informal settlements â CO can accumulate to dangerous levels within minutes.

Mandatory controls: Never operate a fuel-fired furnace in a sealed room. Install roof vents or forced ventilation. Keep furnace doors open during warm-up. If you feel dizzy, nauseous, or develop a headache, shut down the furnace immediately and move to fresh air. Seek medical attention. Train every worker on CO awareness before they enter the foundry floor.

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. Check fuel quality before purchase: Reject wet, dusty, or high-ash fuel. Ask for a moisture content reading or do a simple squeeze test.
  2. Calibrate your air-to-fuel ratio: For coke, aim for 8â10 kg air per kg fuel. For LPG, follow the supplier's stoichiometric ratio (15.5:1 by mass).
  3. Preheat your charge: Use waste heat from the flue to warm scrap before charging. This saves 5â8% fuel per melt.
  4. Maintain a clean coke bed: Replace or screen coke before every heat. Fines and dust choke the bed and reduce airflow.
  5. Monitor flame colour: A neutral flame is blue-white with a short yellow tip. Yellow with black smoke means too much fuel or too little air.
  6. Record every melt: Log fuel weight, charge weight, melt time, and metal temperature. This data is your most powerful cost-control tool.
  7. Inspect tuyeres and blast pipes weekly: Blockages and leaks waste fuel and reduce melt rate.
  8. Train on CO safety monthly: Review symptoms, ventilation checks, and emergency shutdown procedures with all staff.

Further Reading

  • U.S. Department of Energy â Foundry Industry Energy Use (free technical reports on combustion efficiency in foundries)
  • Africa Energy Portal â African Development Bank (fuel pricing, supply chain data, and energy access reports)
  • ILO â Safety and Health in Metal Casting (free code of practice for foundry operations)
  • U.S. EPA â Foundry Area Sources (emission factors and combustion control guidance)
  • Kenya Engineering Registration Board â Foundry Practice Guidelines (regional standards and training resources)

Business takeaway: In African foundries, fuel typically represents 30â50% of variable production cost. A 10% improvement in combustion efficiency translates directly to a 3â5% reduction in total casting cost. The operators who measure, record, and optimise their fuel use will outcompete those who do not. Use this reference as your daily operating guide â not a textbook to be filed away.

quiz.q: What is the approximate melting point of aluminium?
quiz.explanation: Aluminium melts at around 660Â°C.

quiz.q: Which fuel burns hotter and cleaner than firewood?
quiz.explanation: Charcoal is processed wood that burns hotter and with less smoke than raw firewood.

quiz.q: What is a tuyere?
options: B) A pipe that blows air into the fire
quiz.explanation: A tuyere is a pipe or nozzle that delivers air to the combustion zone.

quiz.q: Which colour flame indicates complete combustion?
quiz.explanation: A blue flame shows that fuel is burning efficiently with enough oxygen.

quiz.q: What is a common mistake when starting a furnace fire?
options: B) Using petrol to start the fire
C) Adding small amounts of fuel
quiz.explanation: Using petrol or other flammable liquids is extremely dangerous and can cause explosions.

quiz.q: Why should you store fuel under cover?
options: B) To make it burn faster
quiz.explanation: Wet fuel produces steam and lowers furnace temperature, so it must be kept dry.

quiz.q: What is the recommended thickness of the fuel bed?
quiz.explanation: A fuel bed of about 15-20 cm allows proper air flow and heat retention.

quiz.q: What should you do if you see black smoke from the furnace?
options: C) Increase air supply or use drier fuel
quiz.explanation: Black smoke indicates incomplete combustion; more air or drier fuel will improve burning.

quiz.q: Which fuel is best for melting cast iron?
quiz.explanation: Coke or coal can reach the higher temperatures needed for cast iron (about 1200Â°C).

quiz.q: What safety gear is essential when working with a foundry furnace?
options: B) Leather gloves and face shield
quiz.explanation: Leather gloves and a face shield protect against burns and sparks.

quiz.q: Why is carbon monoxide dangerous?
options: B) It is invisible and deadly
quiz.explanation: Carbon monoxide is odourless and can cause unconsciousness or death in enclosed spaces.

quiz.q: What should you use to start a furnace fire?
quiz.explanation: Paper and kindling are safe; liquid fuels are explosive and dangerous.

quiz.q: What is dross?
options: B) Impurities that float on molten metal
quiz.explanation: Dross is the waste material that forms on the surface of molten metal and must be skimmed off.

quiz.q: How can you estimate the temperature of hot metal without a pyrometer?
quiz.explanation: The colour of glowing metal indicates its temperature: dark red ~600Â°C, bright orange ~900Â°C, yellow-white ~1200Â°C.

quiz.q: What is a common mistake when adding fuel to the furnace?
options: B) Adding large chunks at once
quiz.explanation: Large chunks can smother the fire; it's better to add small amounts frequently.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid using coal with high sulphur content?
options: B) It can ruin the metal and create harmful fumes
D) It is hard to find
quiz.explanation: Sulphur can contaminate the metal and produce toxic sulphur dioxide gas.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a blower in a foundry furnace?
options: B) To supply oxygen for combustion
quiz.explanation: A blower forces air into the fire, providing oxygen for efficient combustion.

quiz.q: What should you do after finishing a melt?
options: A) Pour water on the fire
B) Shut off the blower and let the fire die
quiz.explanation: Shutting off the air and letting the fire burn out is safe; water can cause steam explosions.

quiz.q: Which of these is a safe practice when working with a furnace?
options: C) Having a fire extinguisher nearby
D) Using petrol to start the fire
quiz.explanation: A fire extinguisher or sand bucket is essential for emergency response.

quiz.q: What is the approximate melting point of cast iron?
quiz.explanation: Cast iron melts at about 1200Â°C, requiring high-energy fuels like coke.

quiz.q: Why is it important to preheat a crucible gradually?
quiz.explanation: Sudden heating can cause thermal shock and crack the crucible.

quiz.q: What is a sign of incomplete combustion?
quiz.explanation: A yellow-orange flame indicates insufficient oxygen and wasted fuel.

quiz.q: What should you do if you smell sulphur from the furnace?
options: B) Move to fresh air and stop the process
quiz.explanation: Sulphur dioxide is harmful; evacuate and ventilate the area.

quiz.q: Which fuel is typically more expensive per kilogram in many African markets?
quiz.explanation: Charcoal is often more expensive than coal or firewood due to processing costs.

quiz.q: What is the recommended air supply adjustment when the fire is first lit?
quiz.explanation: Starting with too much air can blow out the fire; increase gradually.

quiz.q: Why should you remove ash from the furnace regularly?
options: A) To make the fire hotter
B) To prevent blockage of air flow
quiz.explanation: Ash can clog the tuyere and reduce air supply, lowering combustion efficiency.

quiz.q: What is a safe way to dispose of ash?
quiz.explanation: Ash can contain hot embers; a metal container prevents fires.

quiz.q: What is the main advantage of using charcoal over coal?
options: B) It produces less smoke and sulphur
quiz.explanation: Charcoal burns cleaner with less sulphur, but may not reach as high temperatures as coal.

quiz.q: What should you do if the flame becomes too yellow and smoky?
quiz.explanation: Increasing air supply provides more oxygen for complete combustion.

quiz.q: Why is it important to work in a well-ventilated area?
options: B) To avoid carbon monoxide poisoning
quiz.explanation: Carbon monoxide can build up in enclosed spaces and cause death.
